Yeah, in the case of Japan it's not so much "western food" as "westernization of diet", but very much that. In other words, while there are KFCs and McDs and the like, it's not that adoption/people running to them is the problem here; but rather the two killers of

  • first world convenience, and crap fast food marketed towards that (be it cup noodles at Family Mart or to-go tendon/tenju/fried foods)

  • And a very real adoption of western-style eating culture: In other words, not hamburgers and fries, but definitely a much higher rate of beef and chicken consumption, that started in the 80s and 90s after lots of other western nations budging in with demanding lower tariffs for cheaper foreign meat (Aus and US mostly).

So it's not McDs and KFC, but rather Japanese food centered on meat dishes the likes of which haven't been seen before 1985/1990, due to the (political chicken-wing-pin negotiation-brought) import of cheap foreign meat.

In the 80s, in my wife's teen years, Korean-style yakiniku (fried meat) places were few and far between, and an excess and treat for the family where they'd indulge on special occasions, or at most like 1-2 times a quarter. Now, there is yakiniku everywhere, and families that eat it weekly (with the working father perhaps eating it 3 times a week with comerades).

The amount of beef, pork and chicken consumption, particularly of import, has blown through the roof in the last 30 years, and in a 5-year-after wake-graph you also see the rise of obesity and obesity-related illnesses like diabetes. No where near US levels, but it's basically at the "watching ripples in the water in the cup in Jurassic Park as the T-Rex stomps closer" levels.

It is absolutely true that people are moving less, and that is an excellent point. It's a messy blend, too, since the above meat deregulation and tariff drops of the 80s and 90s coincide with Japan's rise of console gaming and a stay-indoors culture. (and indeed, in otaku circles that's where I see the most obesity; I see a few gross fat salarymen in thousands in my business district; but when I walk past a gaming or anime event that amount rises dramatically)

Dieticians have even created a new movement here, "Showa 50 Shokuseikatsu", aka "Let's Eat Like it's 1975", basically recognizing that the dietary life (including what was eaten, the amounts, and prep involved) of the pre-cheap-beef pre-80s was the most healthy food culture in Japan in decades; it's seeing wide adoption but the promulgation is still a bit fad-y.

Of course, ultimately, it all amounts to personal growth, recognition, strength and change. But at the same time, there are many foreign meat/sweetener/pharma interests (and Japanese businesses created in their wake that support them) that made billions off of the fattening of Japan over the last 3 (primarily the last 2) decades.

(I recognize that Korea's going to be a bit different, too, as there's been a much deeper culture of beef-based foods historically; but there's indeed a lot of crossover with with lack of activity and sloth-fun)

A lot of the sloth issue here has to do with either studying (for students) or drinking culture (for workers). The students, like I believe it is in Japan, can be out until 11pm or later studying. They have no time to go out and get exercise. When they aren't in classes, they're studying. The most they have time for might be 30 minutes of playing a phone game. For the workers, there are "hweshik" to attend, which are basically company dinners where you're expected to drink until you pass out, essentially. Internet cafes are also big here for young adults and older adults, with a curfew for younger individuals. A lot of people spend their free time gaming as opposed to doing anything active.

Even if you are outdoors, that doesn't mean you're being healthy or active. We have a fashion of hiking gear. You'll have several older people dressed to the nines in hiking gear. They go "climb a mountain", which is really "hiking a hill that even comes with stairs". They do this for a good 15-30 minutes and then have a picnic. Almost always included in these picnics is alcohol.

The diet here definitely contains more meat than before, just like you were mentioning in Japan. There are some religious vegetarians/vegans but it's not very common. Thankfully, it is common enough in some areas that they'll sell vegan meat substitutes. There are also places online to buy canned or bagged meat substitutes. I personally do this. I would even do this if I wasn't vegan because it's not only cheaper but isn't greasy (Koreans like their meat super fatty).
